utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There being no procedural issues, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Situation apparently has changed. Mr. Bakrac, any procedural matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Considering that we are dealing with a videolink, I just wanted briefly for the record to announce some -- a filing and a 54 bis. We have spoken to the Serbian authorities, and we have a response to that. I have talked to Mr. Groome and I just want to inform the Chamber that we are working on it and I think it would be more appropriate to address you tomorrow after the videolink is over. I don't want to take up too much of your time now, because we have this videolink. Or perhaps tonight before the end of working hours I would address you with the 54 bis motion regarding Witness JP-057.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus -- well, Mr. Bakrac, it's not clear to me why this had to be raised at this moment at all, but let's have a look at any filing that is there. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just one comment as to timing. I've substantially reduced the number of questions that I intend to put to the witness. My best guess normally would be approximately one session. There is some unpredictability in the circumstances, but I wanted to let everyone know about that. I did inform the Defence before we began and in case the Chamber wishes to have the next witness ready for the third session or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, of course it depends on Mr. Jordash, whether he has a witness ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We had assumed he was going to start tomorrow. I had arranged to see him this afternoon for a very short conference, but potentially he could be ready. But our preference would be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, preference, but let's use our time. Of course there's always some uncertainty in when another witness concludes his evidence, but I would really appreciate and the Chamber would appreciate if you would seek the witness to be ready later today in case we might finish early.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then good morning to you as well, Mr. Lekovic. Can you hear me, can you see me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. I can hear you very well and I can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire with the booths in The Hague whether the sound quality is better today than it was yesterday. I'm listening to the English channel. I don't have any response yet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then I asked whether the sound quality from the other side of the videolink is better today than it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There's still a lot of interference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent the technicians can help us out, they are invited to do so. We need working circumstances which are good for everyone. Mr. Lekovic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Petrovic, do matters stand as they stood yesterday, that you have no questions for the witness at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus is counsel for the Prosecution. Would you please very much focus your answers on what Ms. Marcus asks you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll try to be as rational in my answers as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lekovic, can you see me and hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you and I can see you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, I have prepared very specific and focused questions for you, all of which, perhaps with the exception of one or two, can be answered with either a yes or a no. If I would like additional clarification, I will ask you, and the Chamber will do so as well. So I request, please, that you do not give explanations in response to my questions but you simply answer yes or no. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You yourself would not have initiated an investigation targeting the accused Stanisic on your own initiative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, Radmilo Bogdanovic would not have undertaken an investigation targeting the accused Stanisic on his own initiative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So it was Zoran Janackovic's initiative exclusively which led to the establishment of the commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, at the insistence of Janackovic, a commission was set up by Radmilo Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You were reluctant to take on the role of president of the commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You felt, as you say in your statement at paragraphs 18 and 19, that since the aim of the establishment of the commission was the aim of Janackovic, that he should preside over the commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggested to Bogdanovic when we were discussing this, and when he informed me that Janackovic was insisting that the commission be set up, he said it would not be good for me to be even a member of the commission, let alone the chairman. And then I said, as undersecretary for state security, Janackovic could be the chairman if the issue at hand was leakage of information from the MUP of Serbia, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And Bogdanovic agreed with you, but Janackovic refused, and thus you were requested to take on that role; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first Radmilo agreed to my proposal, but ultimately he caved in under pressure from Janackovic, and the commission was set up with five members and I was even appointed chairman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Bogdanovic instructed you to carry it out as quickly as possible --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It seems, Your Honour, there's some problem with the videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I think that -- at least I can see the witness at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, can hear me and see me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you now, but I can't see you. I only see Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to repeat my last question. Bogdanovic instructed you to carry out the work of the commission as quickly as possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was written in the decision, to set up the commission which also defined its tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I'd just like to verify whether, in the videolink room, whether it is just a representative of the Registry, the witness, and the technician that is present, because I see people walking around. Could I be informed about ... Could we re-establish the videolink. Restoring the videolink apparently causes some problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is unclear how much time it will take to restore the videolink connection. We will have a break, but everyone is expected to remain standby as the Chamber will remain standby as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps this is the moment you would like to make a submission. We could use the time for that. Please proceed. And there were some submissions to be made by you as well, Ms. Marcus. Let's see -- I hope, as a matter of fact, that there's insufficient time for you to do it, but ... Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we are switching priorities now, but I wanted to ask you, since you suggested to Mr. Jordash that he should bring the witness. I had an agreement last

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought that we were in private session, so I mentioned the name. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Marcus, and I mean no criticism, informed us only this morning that she would take much less time in her cross-examination, and that changes my possibilities of talking to the witness who only arrived yesterday and was proofed by Mr. Jordash, and that's why I wanted to ask the Chamber to delay the witness, not have him start today, but to allow me to speak to him this afternoon. The second thing, why I addressed you with 54 bis motion, the reason is that the National Council for Co-operation has written to you about their talks with us, and since these talks are not resulting in anything for a very long time now, we were asked to inform the Chamber of the outcome, and I thought I should just mention it without taking time away from the videolink. That's why I only took a minute to remind you that this issue is still outstanding. My colleague Mr. Petrovic and I reviewed the documentation regarding JF-057 during the break, and we saw that the Prosecution has received all the documentation that the MUP has at this time, with some redactions. As for our Defence team, we do not need unredacted versions. And if the Prosecution agrees that we use redacted documents and that they be admitted, we can then withdraw our submission under 54 bis. Otherwise, we will require all the documentation unredacted, of course, to be used in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a brief discussion with Mr. -- with the Simatovic Defence this morning. He informed me that he has seen the unredacted document. I would like an opportunity to see specifically the documents that he wants to tender, but I informed him that since it was his exhibit, that he wanted to tender it, that I would not insist on what's underneath the redaction. I would accept his representation that it was simply the name of a person unrelated to this case who filled out the paperwork. If I have an opportunity to confirm that, then the Prosecution will be deferring to the Chamber. I know the Chamber has a particular policy with respect to redactions. It may, in fact, not accept the document in a redacted form. But I informed Mr. Bakrac that I would not insist on a redaction if I had an opportunity to discuss that with him and verify that it was completely relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I think the Chamber would then need a similar confirmation by Mr. Bakrac as what is found under the redactions. And I still do not fully understand why Mr. Bakrac is allowed to look at the -- what's under the redactions and the Chamber would not be, but let's -- if you have an agreement with Mr. Bakrac finally, then you perhaps put it together to the Chamber and then in a kind of a joint motion or joint submission, then the Chamber will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We will discuss this issue. I just wanted to raise the issue of the 54 bis motion in order not to leave you with the impression that nothing is being done and that there is no progress. But I will try to make a joint submission with Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would choose Mr. Groome under these circumstances. But, Mr. Jordash, of course, your position in the matter is not irrelevant either, so if you would please join the gentlemen in their discussions or in their outcome of their discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We have drafted a Rule 54. We're going to file it. I know I said we would file it on Friday, but things got delayed. But we will file it either today or at the latest tomorrow. So it's ready with voluminous annexes dealing with these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll then see what we find in there. And, of course, to the extent matters could be resolved by mutual agreement, of course that's preferred. But of course the Chamber would have its own position in the matter as well. Then let me inquire whether the videolink is restored yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you asked for some time. You had an extension of time for one day. The only thing I'd like to know is whether you are going to address us in open session, which has some consequences for the witness in Belgrade. Because if you address us in private session, we should empty the room in Belgrade in case the videolink would be restored. If you address us in open session, there's no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I do not see any reason why it needs to be in private session. Both those witnesses were -- testified publicly, both DST-070 and DST-072 testified publicly previously; although, I will say that the motion was a confidential motion. So perhaps Mr. Jordash can just confirm that with respect to the UN witnesses, they would be public witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, the intention is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, therefore, no action is in need to be taken in Belgrade. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is an oral response to the motion, the 92 bis motions, filed by the Defence on the 27th of September, 2011, specifically with respect to Witnesses DST-070 and DST-072. The Prosecution does not oppose the 92 bis motion with respect to DST-070. With respect to DST-072, we do oppose the motion but we do not oppose the admission of the testimony and related exhibits of this witness into evidence. However, we seek that the witness be required to appear for cross-examination. In this witness's proposed 92 bis evidence, referring to a video, he says: "So there's Professor Koljevic again. And the people in the military uniforms that he's talking to, they are from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia, not Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I understood that they were a special unit from their Ministry of the Interior. And this is just prior to our release on the 18th of June, and these soldiers or special police were there to provide an escort for us into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." That -- end quote. That is from the Karadzic case, open session, on the 2nd of February, 2011, at transcript 11134. The relationship between this unit and the RS authorities is a key issue in this case. This witness clearly has some knowledge of it, knowledge that was not explored in his prior evidence. He may have significantly more knowledge about how this unit was treated by the RS authorities. For example, he may have witnessed interactions between this unit and the RS military or police units. He may have seen the treatment at check-points, observed the manner in which they crossed borders, observed the demeanour of RS leaders toward them, et cetera. Fairness requires that the Prosecution have the opportunity to examine and test this knowledge. Chambers have identified a number of discretionary factors, militating in favour of a witness appearing for cross-examination. These factors are listed in the Chamber's 7th October 2010 decision on the Prosecution 92 bis motions at paragraph 35. Application of those factors in this case supports the Prosecution's application that DST-072 appear for cross. First, the acts and conduct of the JATD are sufficiently close to the acts and conduct of the accused to make it appropriate for a witness who testifies about them to be required to attend for cross-examination. In this regard, the Prosecution submits that this is similar to the situation of the two Prosecution witnesses who were ordered to appear for cross-examination pursuant to paragraph 51 of the Chamber's 7th October 2010 decision on the Prosecution's 92 bis motions. Second, this evidence does relate to a live and important issue between the parties. The relationship of the DB special unit to the RS authorities is clearly such an issue. Third, this evidence is not cumulative in the sense of Rule 92 bis (A), which defines cumulative evidence as evidence that other witnesses have given in oral testimony. Finally, the issue of the JATD's involvement in the release of the UN hostages was not addressed at all in cross-examination in the prior proceedings in which this witness testified. Therefore, Your Honours, the Prosecution opposes the motion with respect to DST-072 and requests that the witness be called for cross-examination. Your Honour, I have two other brief submissions. If we still have time and if you grant me leave, I would seek to make them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as the videolink has not been restored, we can use our time by hearing further submissions, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The first submission is an order response to the 4th October 2011 motion by the Republic of Serbia for protective measures; that's for DST-052, DST-036, and DST-083. Your Honours have already ruled with respect to DST-052. With your leave, I would present our position with respect to the other two witnesses, DST-036 and DST-083, right now. Thank you. The Chamber announced on the 7th of October that it would take the same approach with DST-052 that was taken with DST-046. That was at transcript page 14194. The Prosecution submits that this approach strikes an appropriate balance between Serbia's interest in protecting its national security and the right of the accused to a fair and public trial. In response to Serbia's motion for protective measures for DST-036 and DST-083, we thus request the Chamber to follow the same approach that it has followed for DST-052 and DST-046. In addition, we note that prior to the Chamber's decision to take this approach we began hearing the evidence of DST-040, provisionally in closed session. We request that the Chamber follow the approach taken for the other witnesses in hearing the remainder of the evidence for DST-040. Finally, Your Honours, this is a brief submission in relation to DST-060. On the 6th of June, 2011, the Stanisic Defence filed summaries for its witnesses. DST-060 was listed as witness number 21 on this list. The witness summary for DST-060 contains a brief paragraph which references only one municipality and the year 1995. According to the filing, DST-060 is scheduled to testify for four hours viva voce. On the 9th of June, 2011, the Prosecution filed an urgent motion related to the non-compliance with Rules 65 ter (G) and Rule 67. In paragraphs 24 and 25 of this filing, the Prosecution outlined the problematic nature of DST-060's witness summary and requested specific relief in paragraph 33(d). At this time, the Prosecution maintains its position with respect to notice provided for DST-060. The Prosecution has not received any statements or proofing notes for this witness. The Prosecution only considers itself generally apprised of very limited facts that relate to one specific location and one year. Based on the foregoing, the Prosecution requests the Trial Chamber to instruct the Stanisic Defence to either provide a witness statement or a more detailed witness summary covering all the issues anticipated to be led through this witness, and allow the Prosecution a reasonable period of time to further investigate any facts that were not part of the original notice for DST-060. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Jordash, if there is any matter on which you could immediately respond, you are invited to do so. For example, the last issue raised about DST-060. But any other matter, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I may address you briefly on DST-060 and also if I may make an application to very briefly reply to the submissions made in relation to DST-072. And I can do the latter within two or three minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as long as the videolink is not restored, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to DST-060, as far as I am aware, his evidence will relate to the one municipality and the one year. That witness is a senior serving police officer and it's been extremely difficult to meet him and obtain any details concerning that evidence. We are in the process of trying to put together a statement to file a Rule 92 ter motion. What I can say is that I sent an e-mail this morning to Belgrade urging them to try again to meet him. With any luck we can meet him in the next few days and he can sign the statement and we can file the statement or serve a courtesy copy immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement is drafted by now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's drafted, but it hasn't been reviewed by the witness. That's the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there is any way that you -- to the extent that the draft statement gives further details, without, of course, going into such a level of detail that the witness has to prove that, because 65 ter summary only reflects what you expect the witness to testify about, it's not a final statement or anything like that, is there any way that you could already meet some of the concerns of Ms. Marcus who apparently is worried about the fact that she has a very short 65 ter summary for four hours viva voce testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure that either we can -- I haven't looked at the latest version of the statement, but I am sure that I can commit to filing at least aspects of that and providing significantly greater detail than the Prosecution have at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say filing, but it's mainly disclosing to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I mean disclosing, sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus, would it be wise to wait for one more day to see what Mr. Jordash is going to reveal to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. And if -- so by tomorrow, is that my understanding, we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, by tomorrow. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By tomorrow. Okay. That's agreed. Any other response, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. In relation to that, no. But if I may just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I may just briefly apply to reply. In a reply, what we would submit, very briefly, is two things. First of all, that the Chamber or certainly the Tribunal's jurisprudence has taken a restrictive view of what constitutes acts and conducts of the accused, and they are defined as personal acts and statements of an accused and do not involve all conduct attributed to or related to an accused or implicating an accused or concerning the underlying conduct or crime-based charged, and I'm citing from Prosecutor versus Galic decision on interlocutory appeal concerning Rule 92 bis, 7th of June, 2002. We submit that the aspect of DST-072's evidence that my learned friend is concerned about is a very, very long way away from the accused's acts and conduct. Secondly, even putting aside that issue, we submit that the aspect of the evidence my learned friend is concerned with is of negligible significance in the case at large. If the witness is called and the witness says - and I think this is my learned friend's concern - the special unit was given preferential treatment, people were respectful to the unit when it crossed the border, it had no problem crossing the border, it was a unit which was clearly treated with a degree of courtesy, if not favour, that will not inform Your Honour of anything other than an agreement had been reached between the Republika Srpska authorities and the Republic of Serbia that this unit would be allowed to escort the hostages to a safe place within Serbia. That's as much as that evidence could ever say. An agreement had been struck. I don't think there's any dispute that an agreement had been struck. We say Mr. Stanisic was pivotal to that negotiation, and as a result of that, all concerned parties had been informed that this unit would remove the hostages and should not be prevented from doing so. That is as much as that witness is ever going to be able to say. That is as significant as that evidence is ever going to be. Those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. We'll consider the matter. I hear promising telephone sounds. I better would have said I hear telephone sounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I would just note for the record at this point, rather than at the end of the witness's testimony, that we have received a partial response to our RFA in relation to this witness, that's Mr. Lekovic, and we are following up on that. As with the other pending partial responses in relation to other witnesses, we may need to seek leave to recall the witness if anything critical turns up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear that you cannot anticipate on what you do not know yet. I wish I could order someone to answer the phone, unfortunately I'm not in that position. We'll -- I'm just thinking about what would be best to do, if we -- I suggest that we take a break, that everyone remain standby. But if the break and if the -- takes more than 20 to 25 minutes, that we would then consider that to be the first long break and make it half an hour. So if the videolink would not be restored before quarter past 10.00 then we would restart as soon as the videolink is restored but not earlier than 20 minutes past 10.00. We have a break of unknown length. --- Break taken at 9.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber had on its mind to immediately proceed, that's why we entered the courtroom. But we -- nevertheless we need three or four more minutes to deal with the matter. And I apologise because this is not the efficiency which we require from the parties, so we are -- it's a clear shortcoming of the Chamber. Is that clear in Belgrade as well, that we take another three or four minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a very short break. --- Break taken at 10.29 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the Chamber still owes you a decision on your last request to postpone the start of the testimony of the next witness. The Chamber has considered it. A similar request was made by Mr. Jordash and was denied. On the basis of your submissions, the Chamber finds no reasons to grant your request, which means that we'll start with the witness as soon as we have concluded the testimony of the present witness. The videolink is working again. The microphone is now switched on, as I see it. Ms. Marcus, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Based upon your analysis in the commission of the analytical materials and the commission's interview with Bogdanovic, there was a conclusion that there had been no wrong-doing on the part of the accused Stanisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to the next series of questions where I intended to mention the names of the other commission members, I discussed with the Defence in advance, they told me that none of them are active members of the service, so I am not going to seek leave to move into private session for those questions. Could we please have Exhibit D288 MFI, not to be shown to the public. Page 30 in English; page 30 to 31 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, at this page in this report which you drafted you discuss the meeting of the commission on the 22nd of May, 1991, the day after interviewing Bogdanovic. And you describe how the commission became polarised. In particular, you wanted to continue the commission's work, whereas the other commission members, Marko Lazovic, Punisa Djuknic or Djukic, and Milun Miljkovic, wanted to wrap it up as quickly and briefly as possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just for the purpose of the record, Mr. Lekovic, we have some documents that name Punisa Djukic as "Djukic" and some as "Djuknic." Which was his correct name or did he use both interchangeably?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his true family name is Djukic. You will find it in the decision on the setting up of the commission which also sets out the names of the commission members. So the name is Djukic, not Djuknic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in fact, there has been other evidence in this case that you and Janackovic were the only ones who wanted to continue the work of the commission after May 1991 and even to restart it in another form. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to emphasise here that Zoran Janackovic and myself were not on the same wavelength, as it were, with this regard. But as the commission president or chairperson, I had to advocate the prolongation of the work of the commission to close the circle, to wrap it up properly, and to provide an adequate evaluation. That's why I insisted that the commission either continued its work or that it be stated that the commission had stopped working and it was up to those who had set it up and who were supposed to evaluate its work to say whether the commission's work was of some use or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You wanted to continue the work of the commission after its final report was submitted in May 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The report that was submitted by the commission to the republican secretary with an accompanying note was signed by all the five members of the commission. In the meantime, the secretary had changed. Bogdanovic was replaced by Sokolovic. And the only thing I requested was for somebody to call up the commission and to say, You did your job as you should have done it and hereby you will stop working. I did not insist on the reinstating of the commission or the continuation of its work because we had provided a report. I just wanted the circle to be closed and that somebody competent, in this case it was the secretary, to hold a meeting with the commission members and Jovica Stanisic and Zoran Janackovic and other people from the top echelons of the MUP. I wanted to hear the secretary to voice his opinion on our work and on our report, and the secretary told me, I don't want to deal with that. Radmilo Bogdanovic started it, that was during his term of office, I don't want to deal with that. So I had to insist, as the president of the commission, although it was started by the previous person, it had to be finished by his successor. And in that sense I insisted not on the continuation of the commission's work. I even said that if the commission's report was not valid and that the new commission had to be set up, that none of the old members should be members of the newly set up commission, that that new commission should comprise new members who would be in a position to draft a better report at the end of their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We understand that you sought an official decision ending the commission's work. My question to you is: The commission as comprised, in fact, ceased functioning after the 23rd of May, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me or Mrs. Marcus, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking anything. Ms. Marcus is putting this question to you. Mr. Lekovic, you -- the questions are put to you through the intermediary of interpreters and sometimes it is a man and sometimes it's a woman. So if you hear a man's voice, it is not my voice but it's the voice of the male interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, I apologise. I'm sorry. The commission submitted its report, you have the date when the report was drafted and when it was forwarded to the republican secretariat with an accompanying note. With that the commission did not cease to exist. This is what I'm trying to explain. It only submitted a report. Somebody was supposed to look at that report and evaluate it. And just like a decision had been made on the setting up of the commission, its tasks and its members, somebody also should have made a decision on the cessation of its work. It should have been done officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, witness, if you would focus on the question that was put to you, is whether "The commission as comprised, in fact, ceased functioning after the 23rd of May ..." So irrespective of whether you considered it necessary to have a decision taken, but whether in fact it ceased working, functioning after the 23rd of May, 1991. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, the fact that it ceased its operations on the 23rd of May, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Milun Mirkovic was not involved in any additional tasks in relation to this subject matter after --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not "Mirkovic," but "Miljkovic."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Pardon my pronunciation. Milun Miljkovic was not involved in any additional tasks --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: He was not involved in any additional tasks in relation to this subject matter after May 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milun Miljkovic was a commission member. He was also an advisor to the chief of administration of the state security for the city of Belgrade. That means that he was my advisor, as a matter of fact. After the 23rd of May, he did not have any particular duties, at least according to what I know as the president of the commission. He was only working on his current tasks, his normal tasks. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Punisa Djukic was not involved in any additional tasks in relation to this subject matter, the subject matter of the commission, after May 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's correct, because Punisa Djukic was the chief of the organisational unit in Sabac, or, in other words, the security centre in Sabac. As far as I know, he did not have any special tasks with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, if you you can please answer my questions with a "yes" or a "no," I would greatly appreciate it. Marko Lazovic was not involved in any additional tasks in relation to this subject matter after May 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is not correct, at least as a commission member and at least according to what I was supposed to know as the commission's president.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Zarko [sic] Kostic was not involved in any additional tasks in relation to this subject matter after May 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not Zarko Kostic. If you look at the decision, you will see that it says Kostic was a commission member and he was also a chief, like Djukic was the chief of the security centre in Sabac. The former one was the chief of the organisational unit in Kraljevo, and a commission member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, witness. Mr. Kostic, it was put to you that he -- Mr. Kostic "was not involved in any additional tasks in relation to this subject matter after May 1991; is that correct?" Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the previous witness -- for the previous name mentioned, Mr. Lekovic, you said that as far as Mr. Lazovic was concerned that it is not correct that he was not involved in any additional tasks in relation to this subject matter after May 1991. Ms. Marcus, are you going to give any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I answered that -- I answered that I don't know, because Marko Lazovic was working in the headquarters of the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you don't know. That's an answer. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: To clarify this, first of all maybe I should correct: It's not Zarko Kostic, it's Zivko Kostic, according to the commission report. That was my error. Now, in terms --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivko, yes, you're right. Zivko is his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: With respect to Marko Lazovic, you are not aware of any activities that he undertook after May 1991 in relation to the subject matter of the commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And then the same would go for Zivko Kostic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that: "When Zoran Janackovic became head of the service, Jovica Stanisic was bypassed whenever that was possible." You were asked: "Why was that?" And your answer was: "It was not only my impression. It was an impression shared by others in the service." This was your impression, you say. When you say "bypassed," do you mean that Janackovic ignored Stanisic at meetings and refused to greet him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did he not greet him, at meetings he tried not to give him a chance to have his voice heard. And then in between the meetings one could see that things were not functioning as they were supposed to function, and the chief of service was the main factor in that kind of non-communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what was the frequency of the interaction between Milun Miljkovic and the accused Stanisic between May and September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milun Miljkovic was still an advisor to the chief of the administration for the city of Belgrade. And Jovica Stanisic obviously had the right to interact and to co-operate. I don't know whether they had any particular conversations, what they spoke about, and they were from the top echelons of their respective services. I really wouldn't be able to tell you what they talked about when they did see each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you are also not able to tell us anything about how many times Miljkovic and Stanisic may have met between May and September of 1991. Do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood my evidence correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Milun Miljkovic engage in any activities in relation to the DB outside of the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: DB in? Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Would you need me to repeat the question, Mr. Lekovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, actually not. Milun Miljkovic, before he became my advisor, was the chief of one of the departments in the Belgrade administration. When he became an advisor to the chief of the administration, he was given certain tasks. I don't know whether he also had tasks that took him out of the DB of Serbia or not related to the DB of Serbia. And the chief of the service in Serbia or somebody from the top echelons had a right to call an operative or one of the leading people and give them a task and by doing so they could circumvent me. In other words, they didn't have to inform me about that. In other words, I can't give you an answer to the question whether Mr. Milun Miljkovic had certain tasks beyond the DB of Serbia or whether he had to perform some duties given to him by somebody.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: My specific question was: Are you aware of any activities that Miljkovic engaged in, in relation to his work within the DB, activities that he engaged in with the DB outside the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. In fact, I didn't know about it, so I can't say anything nor can I give a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, the work of the DB is carried out under a policy of secrecy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the rules of the service and our methodology, most of our activities and work are done in secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that: "... most of the people were happy when Jovica Stanisic was appointed chief of service because everybody knew that he was a professional, somebody who was very familiar with the inner workings of the service ..." You also testified that Janackovic, just like you, was an outsider to the service. Since Stanisic was a professional and experienced DB official and operative and Janackovic was not, it would have been quite easy for Stanisic to continue to carry out covert actions without Janackovic knowing; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just object. I think a time-frame should be given so that we're clear about the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time during which the commission was functioning. Your evidence is that that was April to May, but I would extend the time through to August or September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those words that you are quoting, I wish them to be understood properly. Stanisic is a man who was a career serviceman, starting from the lowest and going to the highest level, did not abuse any of his underlings and he didn't play any games with Janackovic to get to his position as chief of the service, and his work was no secret to anyone in the service. It's secret for the public, but not to Janackovic. It doesn't mean that Janackovic was unable to get Stanisic to get some of the operatives involved in particular tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, what happens now is to some extent the result of what you're asking from the witness. You're asking whether he would have, due to his professional experience against someone who was not a professional, whether he would be able to. So you're asking for a possibility, where, of course, witnesses expect you to ask about their knowledge, what they observed, et cetera. It is a kind of an assessment or judgement you're asking, rather than finding facts. So either rephrase your question or ask for specific facts, whether he has any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will return to this in a different way, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, to your knowledge, there were no DB regulations which would have banned an individual whose work is supervised by a commission from any work, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the commission that I chaired?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Any commission, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no other commissions. We know all very well how the service is regulated, governed by the rules. It's based on the territorial principle. And there were organisational units covering certain territories --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the head office of the service, there were various administrations and lines of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, could you please focus on the question. That is: Was there any rule which banned Mr. Stanisic, when a commission was established, to supervise or investigate his conduct? I mean, a rule which banned Mr. Stanisic from performing his duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due apologies, I must say that the question is phrased a bit strangely. There was no rule that was introduced, introduced then or that existed earlier, to set up the commission in that way with those people. And regardless of the way the question is phrased, I want to say that in the course of the work of the commission there was no rule banning Jovica from appearing at the head office, from showing up at work, occupying his work-place, or receiving his salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday that a suggestion had been made to -- for him to take a vacation while the commission is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer is: "No, such a rule did not exist." And we heard your testimony of yesterday that he could have taken a vacation; he was not required to show up at work by his chief at the time. Ms. Marcus -- Could you again try to focus on the question and first answer that. And if any further explanation is needed, Ms. Marcus will ask you for such explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would like to just refer the Chamber to the evidence of DST-035 at transcript page 12255 to -56 dated the 4th of July, 2011.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, based upon your observations of Jovica Stanisic, did you view him as the kind of operative who would abandon his professional engagements and responsibilities while some political appointees investigate baseless charges against him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question that's a bit more complex, but let me try to give a brief answer. Although there was talk even in the service that a commission had been set up with a task of putting Jovica Stanisic on the carpet and that the chief had something against him, even during the work of the commission Jovica Stanisic remained what he was, a man of integrity. He never interfered with the commission or put any pressure on any member of the commission. He remained honourable and he cared very much about that, which I appreciated a lot. We had graduated from the same university school, although we didn't know each other as students, and the impression I had was that he was very stoic about the decision to set up the commission. He didn't know whether any sort of sanction would be proposed against him or what kind of report the commission would write. So as a man and as a professional of the service, he had my respect for that. And he didn't ever try to impeach me as a political appointee just because I was not one of them. I'm sorry that I had to give a more extensive answer, but the question is rather complex and rather strangely phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, there's no need to comment on how a question is phrased. We leave that to the counsel that put questions to you, or sometimes even the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You are not aware of the extent of the interaction between Slobodan Milosevic and the accused Stanisic during May through July of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no particular knowledge about that, nor did I get involved in any sort of information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You are not aware of any meetings between the accused Stanisic, Goran Hadzic, and Slobodan Milosevic on several occasions between May and August 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I don't know. I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I note for the record the transcript dated 28th June, 2010, at pages 5972 to 5973.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, you are not aware of a May 1991 meeting between Stanisic, Simatovic, Babic, Martic, and Karadzic in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: According to evidence presented in this case, in February or March of 1991 the accused Stanisic, the accused Simatovic, and Milan Martic met with Minister Bogdanovic in his office. You are not aware of this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that meeting ever took place, and I don't know anything about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to Exhibit P978, paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you are also not aware of a meeting in the MUP in Belgrade in Minister Bogdanovic's office between Bogdanovic, Stanisic, and Janko Milakovic which reportedly took place sometime between May and July of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not informed along any line of work, and I don't know if that meeting ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There has been evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before I continue, I refer Your Honours to Exhibit P402, e-court pages 21 to 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There has been evidence in this case that in April 1991 Radmilo Bogdanovic, Janko Milakovic, Ilija Kojic, and the accused Stanisic held a meeting to discuss the establishment of the police force in SAO SBWS. You are not aware of this meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to transcript dated 3rd of May -- 3 May, 2010, at pages 4647 to 4651.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, in fact, you do not have any direct knowledge regarding the accused Stanisic's movements between April and July of 1991; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not my job to know about Stanisic's movements and where he could have been in that period of time, what places he could have visited. He had the position that he had in the service. And as for meetings of the kind you mention, with Radmilo Bogdanovic, I was not invited, nor did I have access to such information, nor did I try to find out. I was not interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So your answer is no, you did not have any such direct knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, no, I did not have any direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You do not have any direct knowledge as to how often the accused Stanisic met with the accused Simatovic between April and July of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period you mention, Simatovic, as far as I'm able to remember, and I can't trust my memory 100 per cent, had some tasks in Kosovo, operative work that took him to Kosovo to collect some information, so I don't know how often and if Stanisic and Simatovic met.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You do not have any direct knowledge as to meetings between the accused Stanisic and Milan Martic between April and July of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in April and May the commission we've discussed was active. And throughout the work of the commission, Jovica Stanisic was at the head office of the service, but I can't say whether he met with Martic or not. I just don't have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, could I again invite you to consider whether you can answer a question by "yes" or "no," because a yes, that it is correct that you have no direct knowledge, appears from your answer. Ms. Marcus is trying to be very focused and trying to be as efficient as possible, could you please assist her. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, you do not have --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to respond to this. If we are talking about the period of April and May, we're talking about Jovica Stanisic from two different angles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was in the sights of the commission that I led --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you here. The answer -- it appears clearly from the answer that you have no direct knowledge; therefore, what Ms. Marcus did put to you was correct and you could have just confirmed that. If at the end of your testimony you think that we are missing something which is very important, then you may have one or two or three minutes to address those matters. Ms. Marcus, please proceed. And, Mr. Lekovic, please refrain from commenting on rulings I give. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, you do not have any direct knowledge as to how often the accused Stanisic travelled to Knin between April and July of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I don't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You do not have any direct knowledge as to how often the accused Stanisic travelled to the SBWS region of Croatia between April and July of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In fact, you do not actually have any direct knowledge regarding the activities of the accused Stanisic between April and July of 1991; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But despite all the criticism I received from Mr. President, I must say I did not have the duty to know about the movements of Mr. Stanisic. And I do not have that knowledge. That's my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, no one talks about you having a duty. We are interested in what you observed, whether you have any direct knowledge. You are not in any way criticised for whether or not you had to do any such thing. Let that be clear. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I refer the Chamber to Exhibit D270, paragraph 58; D271; and D289. As well as to the transcript at the 30th of June, 2011, at pages 12179 to eight -- to -80, in reference to the work of the commission. Thank you, Mr. Lekovic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I do think what my learned friend has just done -- I don't think the witness needs to hear this, but I do think what my learned friend has just done in listing transcripts is somewhat unfair. I don't know what these transcripts say. I don't know what the relevance is to my learned friend's cross-examination. We were not, as far as I'm aware, told what the relevance is. And, in fact, what we've had is a long list of questions of what the witness isn't aware of without saying from the Prosecution what it is they say Stanisic did and what it is the witness failed to notice or was not in a position to notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, whether it's fair or unfair, I would say, first of all, what Ms. Marcus did is to inform the Chamber about the context in which we -- in which she put the questions to the witness. Of course, I do not know them either. I think, as a matter of fact, it's perfectly fair for you to know that already at this point in time that Ms. Marcus will connect the answers to other evidence and even give you an opportunity now to look at that evidence so as to assist you in preparing for any further questions in re-examination. That's one. Second, if I remember well, you always very much insisted, whether or not the Chamber supports that position, that the Prosecution should always put to the witness or at least elicit from the witness evidence on what they could possibly tell about what apparently would be, if the witness knows, either in support of or contradicting its case. I think, to that extent, Ms. Marcus has done what you insisted. And, again, I'm refraining from any position of the Chamber in this respect. What you always urged the Prosecution to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was to put a positive case, not do what has just happened, which is to put what the witness isn't aware of but without saying what it is the witness should have been aware of or might have been aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If what Ms. Marcus did is to explore whether the witness has any knowledge, knowledge that could possibly contradict the Prosecution's case, in which case if this is at least to be considered as eliciting evidence in support of the Prosecution's case rather than to deal with matters which were touched upon in chief, but if the witness says, I do not know, lack of knowledge is not contradicting the Prosecution's case as far as I can see now, because the Prosecution's case is not that Mr. Lekovic has knowledge about certain activities, but the Prosecution's case is about activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour's completely -- I can see Your Honour is completely against me, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not against you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But what I would, just for the record, say, that in our submission what the right approach would have been, to identify what the Prosecution's case is in relation to meetings and so on with various prominent people, put it to the witness in a concrete form, and allow Your Honours to see what, if anything, the witness could say about it and so that Your Honours could understand properly the witness's lack of knowledge and the significance of it. But I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, I object against a expression that I would be against you. I certainly disagree with you; that's a bit different phrasing. The matter, of course, is a matter which has come up many, many times. The Chamber has asked the parties for guidance on how to conduct cross-examination, especially in relation to Rule - what is it? - 90(H)(ii), I think it is. That guidance or that decision is about to be issued. So therefore you'll find the Chamber's position in relation to these matters in quite some detail in a decision which is in its latest stages of preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I meant nothing when I said that Your Honour is against. It's an English phrase, and old habits die hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's accepted, Mr. Jordash. Then Prosecution has no further questions. Mr. Bakrac, have the questions by the Prosecution triggered any need for you to put additional questions to the witness -- or to put questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still don't know. I did not want to interrupt my learned friend, Ms. Marcus. However, on pages 31 and 32 when Ms. Marcus asked him about various meetings, she also provided us with references to P evidence. However, she asked the witness about a meeting that took place in May 1991 involving Babic, Karadzic, Martic, and others in Sarajevo, that's pages 2, 3, 4 and 5. We were not provided with a reference. She did not tell us what the basis was for the question. We would like to be provided with the reference. We would like to look at the document during the break. And since the witness responded and said that he remembers where Mr. Simatovic was in 1991, we might have questions for the witness, but we don't have any references as to the basis for the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could you assist Mr. Bakrac? Or was it that you just wanted to exclude ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour, to find that and provide it to him within the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other questions at this moment, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Apart from this, we have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a request to be given two additional minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, it's your witness. Would you -- perhaps it would be good to give the witness an opportunity to say something for two minutes so that you -- if it triggers any need for further questions, that you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And I would then apply for a short adjournment to just check these transcripts to see if there's anything there which I'd like to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's first give an opportunity to the witness. You asked for two minutes, Mr. Lekovic. I'm very generous; I grant you four minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, for this time. But in the interests of truth and justice, I accepted to testify as a Defence witness because I was a member of the commission that we discussed. Second, Madam Prosecutor, Mrs. Marcus, put certain questions to me that I found confusing and I understood they were tendentious, and they tend to disqualify my evidence yesterday and today. This insistence on those meetings and saying that Stanisic was somewhere, in some places, with some people, I want to support Mr. Wayne in his comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, Mr. Lekovic, I'm going to stop you. I gave you an opportunity to bring further information you have available to our attention. I did not give you the four minutes to comment and criticise on the way in which the examination was conducted. Please, please. There was one matter which, however, may be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, would you -- please do not interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, there was one observation you made which was about questions being confusing. If there's any question that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tendentious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Lekovic, I limited my observations to what you said about confusing questions. If there has been any question which was confusing you, I would have expected you to ask for a clarification so as to take away the confusion. If there's any question at this moment you remember that you -- that confused you and where you would like to seek clarification in order to verify whether the answer you've given is given in a right understanding of what the question was, you may specifically address any such questions. Apart from that, you can add whatever knowledge you have about the events at the time which you consider necessary for us to know, and you are not allowed to comment and criticise on the way in which the parties have conducted their cross-examination. So, please proceed. Do you have any question clearly on your mind which you say that confused you? because then I'll invite the party that put that question to you to put it again to you in a clearer way. Is there any such question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you again for the time you have given me. I agree with Mr. Wayne and I think that some questions -- I'm not criticising the Prosecutor, I'm not criticising Madam Prosecutor who put questions to me on behalf of the Prosecution, but some of the questions were not fair. From the aspect of my role as a witness, I'm not here to testify about all areas. I'm not here to answer all of the different questions. And as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, Mr. Lekovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would -- I wanted us to understand each other. I wanted to clarify things in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lekovic, I specifically asked you whether there was any question that you now remember confused you so that it can be put again to you. If questions are unfair, it's the other party - that is, if these are questions by the Prosecution, it will be the Defence; or if it is the Defence, it will be the Prosecution - which will object to such a question considered to be unfair. Therefore, I repeat my question to you: Do you remember at this moment any question you considered was confusing you which may have impacted on your answer? So I'm not seeking any general comments on questions, but whether there was any specific question you now say, That confused me. Please tell us what questions it was, and I'll invite the parties to put that question again to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a question about my knowledge about a meeting in Radmilo Bogdanovic's office where Stanisic, Martinic [as interpreted], and others were present; that was one confusing witness [as interpreted], and the interpretation was that the witness was not aware of the meeting hence the answer was incomplete. I was confused about that as well as with the questions about Krajina and ... just bear with me, please. So those questions were confusing, and my answers were not -- I was not avoiding answers. I was surprised that my answers were interpreted as the witness not being aware of things or that the witness was avoiding to provide an objective or correct answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any concern about the translation of your words, then -- and we have native-speaking persons here who will draw the attention of the Chamber to that and seek a correction of the translation if the need be, Mr. Lekovic. The question about the -- a meeting in Radmilo Bogdanovic office. Ms. Marcus, you put that question to the witness. Could you perhaps put that question to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One moment, please, just to verify. There were two questions relating to two separate meetings in Minister Bogdanovic's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please revisit that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I will do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The question was: "According to evidence presented in this case, in February or March of 1991 the accused Stanisic, the accused Simatovic, and Milan Martic met with Minister Bogdanovic in [the minister's] office. You are not aware of this; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So in order to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not -- you have no awareness of such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know about it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still do not know what was confusing in the question. But the other question, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, the other question was: "And --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: "... you are also not aware of a meeting in the MUP in Belgrade in Minister Bogdanovic's office between Bogdanovic, Stanisic, and Janko Milakovic which reportedly took place sometime between May and July of 1991; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You link that with the issue of Baranja and the problem of Baranja, so my answer is this: I didn't know about the meeting, but I was surprised that you insisted on me answering whether they discussed the issue of Baranja or what, and that's why I saw that question as confusing. That's how I understood the question, as being confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what you do, as a matter of fact, you -- you interpret the question and link it to matters which are not in the question itself. You have no awareness of that meeting; that seems to be clear from your answer at this moment. The Krajina questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There was a question about SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The question was: "There has been evidence in this case that in April 1991 Radmilo Bogdanovic, Janko Milakovic, Ilija Kojic, and the accused Stanisic held a meeting to discuss the establishment of the police force in the SAO SBWS. You are not aware of this; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that confusing questions turn out to be less confusing. But, Mr. Lekovic, is there any information in relation to the questions that were put to you which you consider important for the Chamber to know? I'm not asking for impressions or judgements or opinions. But if you would know that a certain event took place which is directly to be connected with the questions that were put to you, you have an opportunity to inform us about such information which is within your knowledge. But wait a second to add anything until counsel has concluded his consultations with Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Jordash --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have dealt with the confusing questions. I gave an opportunity to the witness to add anything in his direct knowledge which he considered important for us to understand his testimony. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to give Mr. Bakrac the reference he was seeking before with respect to the meeting in Sarajevo. I apologise for not citing that specifically in my cross. The reference is to Exhibit P1878, which corresponds to the testimony of that witness in the Milosevic case at page -- at Milosevic transcript page 13082, which is contained within P1878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps a little note would have served better, because this might really confuse the witness. Mr. Lekovic, I invited you to add any information, any -- within your direct knowledge. You have an opportunity to do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will that be my final word or will there be more questions put to me after that? Will that be my final address before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not invited to address the Trial Chamber. You're invited to add any piece of information you consider important in relation to the answers you've given. And Mr. Jordash will have some further questions for you after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to what I provided in my written statement and the answers I provided yesterday and so far today, I have nothing to add. I will be prepared to answer any new questions after the break, if there are any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll now take that break, and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, being provided with the sources, any questions for the witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We know that the witness is 92 quater witness and we don't see a need to put any questions to this witness. Therefore, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not call him a 92 quater witness because he is on our screens, so he is available, to be silent on the -- on that worse situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assume that you understood that the reference was referred to as 92 quater. God forbid that I refer to this witness as a 92 quater, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please. I haven't as yet managed to see all the transcripts. I'm hoping that the remaining ones are going to be brought to me, but I can begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's get started. Further question will be put to you, Mr. Lekovic, by Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At transcript 34, during the questions by Ms. Marcus, you noted that Mr. Stanisic was in the sights of the commission that you led, and I just want to ask you a little more about that to seek clarification of what that means or meant. First of all, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, D450 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- at paragraph 12, you noted that Janackovic was sending information to Milosevic three times a day. Could you just indicate when that was? Was this during the time of the commission or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD LEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let's understand each other. Maybe I have received an erroneous translation. I did not say that Stanisic was targeted by commission, but, rather, that he was in sight of the commission. The commission was primarily set up because of Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Janackovic insisted.
